P1.evidence: Acknowledged the application honestly, including what was missing from it — 'I saw your application. It was very intriguing, but there was not much information over there.' The open question was clean and specific: 'So walk me through, like, what's been going on? What's the main thing you're looking to fix right now?' But no frame was set at all — nothing about where you are, where you want to go, what's in the way and what you need — and consequently no agreement was asked for. The call ran on rapport instead of structure from the first minute, which is why it took until minute 38 to discover that the prospect had no cash.

P2.evidence: The most complete baseline in the batch. Age was asked outright ('How old are you?'), and height and weight came out of a well-placed goal question ('what's the ideal weight you would like to hit?'). Work, travel cadence and desk-bound status were all established. The injury probe was the best example in the corpus — the open question, then two targeted follow-ups: 'Any stiffness that appear maybe in your shoulder traps?' and 'How about lower back?' — which is what surfaced the hips and the knee. Training was asked, diet was asked in detail and the prospect recited a full day of meals, and sleep and energy were asked together, which is what surfaced the narcolepsy. Only P2c falls short: there was no general health-conditions question, so a diagnosed neurological condition arrived by luck through an energy question rather than by being asked for, and nothing hereditary was ever explored.

P3.evidence: Four of the eight moves ran and the ladder still stopped one rung short of anywhere useful. The target-weight question, the missing-sport question ('what are you missing?'), the why question ('What would be your biggest why for that?') and the future-projection question ('when you make that transformation, what becomes possible for you?') were all asked properly, and the reflect-back landed cleanly — 'Would it be correct to say that kind of a structure, that you need a structure for that?' / 'Yeah, for sure.' The failure is P3f and P3g. The deepest answer the rep obtained was productivity at work, and he accepted it as terminal: 'the number one priority for me right now is build our brand.' Nobody asked who else this impacts or drove through to identity, mortality or legacy, on a call with a man turning 40, single, who has moved every three months for fifteen years and has not played a sport in a decade. The material was sitting there and the phase stopped at business efficiency.

P4.evidence: Barely run. What have you tried before, what happened and what is the one thing in the way were never asked. The prospect named his own root cause twice, unprompted — 'because I couldn't get consistency down... I wasn't ever home, wasn't able to just like, cook good meals' and later 'when I'm all over the place and inconsistent, I'm very unproductive' — and the rep took it without developing it. The nearest thing to a probe was the incredulous 'did you play any sports for the past two years?' which is a fact-check, not a root-cause question. This matters more here than on most calls because the prospect had already solved the problem himself since April without help, so the case for paying $6,000 depended entirely on establishing why self-direction will fail him again, and that case was never built.

P5.evidence: No consequence frame at any point. Nothing about what the next two years look like if nothing changes, nothing about whether he is willing to settle, nothing about a line in the sand — which is striking given he had just described losing ten years to exactly that drift. The only urgency deployed came after the price, was seasonal rather than personal, and was weak: 'you're in a best spot right now for the summer... It will be a bummer and waste to not use this momentum before the autumn comes.'

P6.evidence: The all-in question was asked in the right place, before anything was presented: 'if we can figure out all the details, are you going to be fully committed to showing up and doing the work to hit those goals?' — answered 'Yeah, I think I can do that for six months.' He then moved forward on a clear yes. Two blemishes. The rep undercut his own question before asking it — 'I don't think I need to ask that' — which invites a soft answer, and he got one, 'I think I can'. And the belief question was never asked.

P11.evidence: Payment was genuinely attempted — two financing application links were sent live in the chat and the prospect opened both — but nothing was collected and no decision was reached. The Trevor onboarding call was mentioned as the destination twice ('get you onboarded on a call with Trevor, and you're going to be off to the races') and never scheduled. The agreement was never mentioned, and neither was the welcome email, the Skool community link or the onboarding questionnaire. The one thing done right at the end was pinning a specific callback time rather than leaving it open — 'I'll call you tomorrow in the morning' at around 9am — though even that was verbal, with no calendar invite sent.

objection_plays.detail: The only call in this batch where the isolation move ran, and it ran correctly and immediately: 'apart from the finances, everything cool? Anything else that would be stopping you from being 100% in?' — answered 'No, I don't think so.' He then asked the monthly-surplus question. From there it fell apart. No cash on hand, no number of credit cards, no available credit per card, no used-versus-available, and — most conspicuously on this particular call — no question about investments, when the prospect had just volunteered that he and four partners own 90% of a company with a strong valuation. The script explicitly asks about crypto, stocks and investments and the rep skipped it in front of the largest asset on any call in the batch. Instead of building the picture he routed to third-party consumer credit, and when that did not clear the budget he cut the scope to a three-month tier.

'Let me think about it, give me a day' was met with a seasonal urgency line and a pinned callback, which is the useful half. None of the scripted moves ran: no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you to your goal', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'so what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no identity move. Given the prospect had already conceded 'four hundred over twelve, that actually fits your budget', the gap between fitting and buying was exactly the thing OA exists to close and it was left unexamined.

Clinical fit, and an unusually specific one. The prospect disclosed diagnosed narcolepsy, that he is currently off all medication in a six-month trial, and that he is substituting nicotine patches for prescribed stimulants. The rep's entire response was 'Okay. Okay. All right.' No question about sleep attacks under load, no question about whether the neurologist has been asked about resistance training, no adjustment to the programme description that followed. The script has no clinical screen at all, so nothing prompted him — but overhead ballistic work with an unmedicated narcoleptic is a foreseeable harm the process should catch.

Illiquid founder, a category the money play does not contemplate. Objection C assumes wealth is either in cash, on cards or in tradeable assets. This prospect's wealth is equity in a private company he deliberately starves of dividends — 'you can't take a valuation to the bank right now, so we all take very low salaries.' There is no scripted move for it, and the rep's fallback, consumer instalment credit, put the total cost above the cash price. Worth a script addition: for founders, ask about the business's ability to pay, not the individual's.

notes: The strongest baseline and the weakest case-building in the batch — Phase 2 was near-perfect and Phases 4 and 5 barely happened, so a man who had already lost 22 lb on his own was asked for $6,000 without anyone establishing why he needs help. Coach the money sequence: the isolation question was run correctly for once, then abandoned after one question in favour of third-party credit. Ask about the company before reaching for Klarna.
